name: Nature, Beauty and Mood
description: Faithful replication of Study 2 of Meidenbauer, Stenfors, Bratman, Gross, Schertz, Choe and Berman (2020), Journal of Environmental Psychology, "The affective benefits of nature exposure: What's nature got to do with it?", with the authors' six validated image sets (OSF ehtk9). Each participant is randomly assigned to one set of 45 photographs: very high, high or low aesthetic value nature, or high, low or very low aesthetic value urban (high and low sets are matched on prior preference across nature and urban). Mood is measured before (T1) and after (T2) viewing with the 6-item STAI (calm, relaxed, content; upset, tense, worried; 1 = not at all to 4 = very much, items in random order) and four 1–100 visual analogue scales (happy, sad, inspired, angry, random order). Each photograph stays on screen at least 7 s before the 1–7 preference rating (strongly dislike to strongly like) unlocks; rating moves to the next photograph. In the original (615 MTurk adults), nature and urban sets matched on aesthetic value produced no difference in affect change; instead, each participant's own liking of the images predicted the change, and the largest benefit followed the very high aesthetic value nature set. Condition codes, STAI composites and mood scales match Study2_data.csv; image keys match the set folders and Study1_image_sets_prefRatings.csv. About 10 minutes. Differences from the original study: (1) the brief nature-connectedness measure given before T1 (not analysed in the paper) is left out; (2) the wording of the four mood scales ('How happy do you feel right now?', ends 'not at all' / 'extremely') is ours, the paper gives only the labels; (3) photographs resized to at most 1280 px; (4) condition drawn at random per participant, not balanced. Images from the SUN database and non-copyrighted web searches, as shared by the authors; used with credit and removed if the authors object.

config.description: Is it nature, or just beauty, that lifts our mood? Each participant is assigned to one of six image sets of 45 photographs: very high, high or low aesthetic value nature, or high, low or very low aesthetic value urban scenes (matched on prior preference ratings). Mood is measured before and after viewing with a 6-item STAI (calm, relaxed, content; upset, tense, worried) and four 1–100 scales (happy, sad, inspired, angry). Each photograph stays on screen at least 7 s and is rated from strongly dislike (1) to strongly like (7). Rebuilt from Study 2 of Meidenbauer, Stenfors, Bratman, Gross, Schertz, Choe and Berman (2020), Journal of Environmental Psychology, with the authors' image sets from OSF ehtk9.
